speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a brief contribution to this debate it gives me great pleasure to welcome back to this house the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). He is a very active minister and I predicted that something would happen to him if he did not take things easier, but I was not thinking of an accident of the kind

that did befall him. In January he came to visit the military units in my city. It was a cold day, although not quite as cold as it is to-day. He was reviewing the troops when the thermometer registered 21 degrees below zero with a thirty-mile gale. I went up to call on him and I prophesied a severe attack of pneumonia if he did not watch his step. We are glad indeed to see him back, restored to health and ready to take up the onerous duties he has to perform.
I desire to make some brief reference to the speech from the throne. It is rather colourless; there is nothing very startling in the government's programme. Nearly all the major proposals have been anticipated already by the general public and by the press. I am glad to know that we are being spared the indignity of another plebiscite and that sort of thing; so that I shall not devote much time to a discussion of the subject matters referred to in the speech, although some of them require elucidation.
Reference is made to a joint committee representative of Canada and the United States to coordinate the efforts of the two countries in agricultural production. I regretted that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) did not touch on this important matter during the course of his remarks. I am not condemning him; I am simply saying that the house and the country should be told at the earliest possible moment just what these proposals are.
There is also the matter of the Canadian war supply board. In the resolution standing on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) reference is made to the establishment of a Canadian war supplies allocation board. I understand that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) is to be the chairman of that board, and that it is to be made up of members of the cabinet. We shall await with considerable interest the statement of the minister in this regard. I assume he will make it at an early day, possibly on that resolution if not during this debate. The house should be told just what this proposal is and what is intended. It is a new departure, a departure that carries with it implications of great good in the common cause. More than that I shall not say at the moment, except that I shall await with interest the government's proposals.
Then there is the paragraph written by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the seclusion of his own sanctum sanctorum. He utters this pious hope:
Every effort must be made to ensure, after the close of hostilities, the establishment in

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) .
useful and remunerative employment, of the men and women in our armed forces and in war industries.
I think we can all reecho that. But as to the ways and means of doing it we are left entirely in the dark. How is it to be accomplished? We are not told. May I remind the Prime Minister and the members of this house that in a magnificent address delivered within the last few days, to which I am sure nearly all of us listened, the President of the United States told his people and the world at large that private industry and private enterprise would provide the great bulk of employment after the war, to be supplemented by appropriate congressional legislation and action. He made bold to make that assertion, and so it will be in Canada, notwithstanding all the isms and all the talk that is going around in this and that circle as to the world that is to be. There is nothing that will take the place of private enterprise in our economic system.
I have not looked into the constitutional history of the development of what is known as the speech from the throne, but my memory indicates that it had a definite purpose in the days of long ago. To-day it is a truism to say that quite often the speech from the throne is used as an instrument to conceal rather than to reveal the government's intentions. I think that can be said with some degree of truth with respect to this speech from the throne. I have sometimes wished it were possible under our constitutional set-up that our speech from the throne could be patterned on the address which the President of the United States gives to his nation at the opening of a congressional session and in which he dilates upon the state of the union and gives a lead to the nation. I quite appreciate that with us this may not be possible, since we have not in Canada the same separation that there is between the legislative and executive functions in the United States. This is just a suggestion which arose in my own mind, because I have been convinced that the speech from the throne does not mean very much in Canada. I am certain that there is great opportunity for improvement.
I should like to turn for a moment to a consideration of the war position. As I read the speech, more than once, I felt that sufficient emphasis had not been placed upon the fact that this world-wide war has not yet been won.	I believe the Prime Minister
during the course of his remarks in this debate endeavoured to bring us back to a sense of reality, but I am afraid, and I hope I will be pardoned for saying so, that the Canadian people do not listen very much
these days to the Prime Minister with respect to matters of that kind.

In most of the speeches in this debate, if not all of them, I have sensed a lack of appreciation of the fact that the end of this devastating conflict is still far off. It would seem that some of us are more concerned with post-war conditions and political manoeuvring than we are with the vital task of winning this war-and that goes perhaps for all of us. For three long years Britain and her dominions were on the defensive. Then the great United States came into the conflict. In November last, and not until then, with the invasion of North Africa we began to see a gleam of light over the hill top-the end of the beginning, as Mr. Churchill so aptly put it. Since then in Russia, in the southern Pacific, in Africa and in other theatres of war our gallant forces have steadily gone forward. But I suggest to hon. gentlemen that the victory is still far ahead. One thing has emerged, and perhaps we can be in agreement on this, that as the allied nations have taken the offensive the danger of invasion of this continent is receding. But we have not yet won the battle of the Atlantic. The U-boat menace-and I want to be careful in what I say about this-is as great to-day as it was at any other time in the history of the war. The battle of Tunisia is not yet won; it is only beginning. I predict it will be a long and a hard battle, but it is a battle which must be won before there can be a successful opening of a second front in Europe. It may be months before Rommel is driven into the sea, as Mr. Roosevelt so graphically predicted the other night. Notwithstanding the magnificent, the marvellous progress of the Russian armies, the battle of Russia is not yet won. Our gallant Russian allies have not yet recovered all the territory that nazi Germany took from them in
446	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
the summer of 1942. But I am happy, as I know we all are, to pay tribute to them for the magnificent victories which they have already won over German arms at Stalingrad and elsewhere, and to wish them godspeed on their way.
While it is all right to talk about the world that is to be after this conflict is over, and to begin now to plan to win the peace, I say with all the earnestness at my command: let us concentrate on winning the war; let us keep our eye on the ball; for winning the war is the first and foremost objective of this nation and of every other one of the allied nations. All other matters are in point of time and in substance relatively unimportant.
On this issue of the winning of the war the position of the party to which I have the honour to adhere is clear and unequivocal, and always has been, and please God always will be until the last gun is fired. I have proclaimed that objective many a time during the three sessions I had the honour of leading this party. From that objective I have never wavered and this party has never wavered. Recently at Winnipeg this party reaffirmed its position in the following words-I am going to put them on Hansard so that all who read may understand:
We pledge to the men and women in the services at home, abroad and at sea, support to the limit of our resources, to the end that they shall be adequately 'supplied with reinforcements, equipment and munitions of war in order that they can and shall be so employed in cooperation with our fighting allies that Canada shall make her due and honourable contribution to a common and complete victory.
There is nothing equivocal about that. And further:
Recognizing that the world struggle in which Canada is engaged requires a total war effort, we believe in compulsory national selective service, and that all those selected to serve in the armed forces should be available for service wherever required. We believe in the effective total utilization and proper allocation for war, by compulsion where necessary, of all the resources of Canada, including agriculture, industry, and finance, as well as man-power, and that our aim should be at all times to bring about so far as human means can achieve it, an equality in sacrifice.
We stand by that declaration, Mr. Speaker, and by it this party shall be judged. We believe in the principles enunciated in those two paragraphs, and we commend them to the people of Canada.
With many of the topics raised in this debate, I have not time to deal, but I cannot refrain from making a brief reference to the speech delivered the other evening by my old friend the member for Richelieu-Vereheres (Mr. Cardin). What I shall have

to say in this regard is said in all kindness and without intent to wound or to injure; I hope no word of mine will be constructed as having been so intended. I regret that the hon. gentleman is not in his place to-day.
First let me say that with many of the views which the hon. gentleman expressed, those, for example, relating to methods of government by order in council while parliament is in session, those relating to certain regimentations and forms of control, and especially those relating to the supremacy of parliament, I am in hearty accord. But I was much pained at what he said near the conclusion of his address, in what I believe was the main portion of his address, with respect to Canadian participation in this war. As I heard him I thought: This is isolationism in the nth degree, this is isolationism stark naked and unashamed, I wondered whether his views reflected those of his compatriots whom he represents in this House of Commons. If they do, then let us say good-bye to national unity in Canada; for it indicates a dangerous situation which must be faced by every one of us who loves Canada and desires to see it prosper, everyone who would like to see the two great races in this country go forward hand in hand to build up this country and have it do its, full duty. If the views which he expressed are the considered opinion of the people who sent him here, there is not much hope for this nation. The school of thought which he represents in that connection is as far apart as the poles from the school of thought to which I adhere in this great conflict. I shall not say more in that regard, except that I regret the attitude on the part of the hon. gentleman, and I regret it the more if he represents any very considerable body of public opinion in his province and among his compatriots.
But, on reflection, I am not really surprised. As a student of public affairs I know, and we all know, that since 1917, for more than twenty-five years, he under the leadership of my right hon. friend taught his people day in and day out that Canada, if ever called upon to fight in battle, should think and fight only for her own defence and for her own salvation. That, I submit, is an unworthy attitude.

I should like to refer briefly to the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). The minister made an able but, may I say, an ex parte defence of his administration in the agriculture department and the food situation in Canada. A calm reading of that speech will disclose many fallacies in his argument. I have only time to refer to one or two. On the question of shortages and surpluses I put this conundrum to the house after listening to the Minister of Agriculture; when is a surplus not a surplus? When is a shortage not a shortage?

I did the hon. gentleman the honour, or-I will put it this way-I did myself the honour of listening attentively to his speech; I read it as well, and as I say, it was an able but ex parte exposition of his position. We really have only one great surplus in this country, and that is of wheat and other grains. We have no large surplus of butter, but we have a sufficiency. It is apparent that, for reasons, there is a shortage of beef, but I suggest that if the price ceiling policy of the government were not so sacrosanct there would be an ample supply of beef in this country.
What is happening? The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Mills) intimated the other day that there was a black market in beef.

Is there a black market in beef? I know this, that if the wartime prices and trade board will allow the price of beef on the hoof to rise to twelve cents a pound there will be an ample supply for everybody. And why should not the farmer, the primary producer, who has gone for so many years without his fair share of the national income, now, at a time when there is an abundance of purchasing power in this country, get a fair return for his beef?
There is no shortage of butter, but the butter situation is spotty. There are shortages in some communities and surpluses in others. In my own province there is no shortage of butter, but a grave injustice is being done to one-half of the producers of butter in my province by reason of a system under which the price structure is being buttressed by the
bonus system. Half the production of butter in New Brunswick is through the creameries, and half is home processed butter: the one is given the advantage of ten cents per pound bonus on butter fat, and the other class of producer is denied it.

The party across the floor was licked once on butter, and history might repeat itself. They are slipping, but they don't know it.

I do not wish to say anything more on that point, because I am just realizing how short my time is.
There is another topic, however, to which I desire to refer, and that is the man-power problem. I see the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) in his seat. It will be recalled that on March 23 of last year the Prime Minister, after voting down the amendment I had the honour to move in this house three or four weeks previously setting forth a substantive, affirmative motion which would lay down a definite principle for dealing with this question of man-power qua agriculture, industry and the armed forces, announced the establishment of the national selective service and defined its scope and policy. Coupled with that announcement, or at about the same time as that announcement was made, came the appointment of Mr. Elliott Little as director of national selective service. Mr. Little came to Ottawa amid the acclaim of the government and all the government propagandists. Most people, I fancy, thought that the government did have a real policy in relation to this vital question of manpower, and they were expecting to receive and ready to receive a definite lead on the question. I have no doubt that when Mr. Little came to Ottawa he too thought that the government had a policy. At all events I believe he entered upon his duties with the good will of everybody, including, if I may say so, organized labour itself. The next step in this tragedy of errors was the man-power speech which the Prime Minister

delivered over the radio on August 19, in which he told of an extension of that policy. I quote his words:
... in order to put every competent man and woman to work in essential industry.
I believe I am correctly quoting him. Mr. Little went to work. \Ve had a new minister of labour under and with whom Mr. Little was to work. I ask this question in view of the disclosures of last summer: How much help did Mr. Little get from his minister?

Possibly it may have been for one reason, but I suggest to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), who has interrupted me, that it was necessary that he should stay at home and work out the government's policy on national selective service, and that was not done. Mr. Little told the sad story in his lengthy memorandum made public on the return of the minister and on his resignation. I have not the time to go into all the details, but that statement shows conclusively that the man-power policy of the government as announced by the Prime Minister was a delusion. The government had no real policy.

If it had, it refused to give governmental direction, and that is one of the charges Mr. Little made against this administration; and what was called a man-power problem was really a man-power muddle. I am not coining these phrases; these phrases were coined by the oldest liberal journal of the maritime provinces, the Halifax Chronicle, in discussing this matter. And a muddle it has remained ever since. That is the consensus of opinion of the people of Canada.
The Prime Minister, so far as I can recall, has never made any statements publicly since the Little resignation. I was given to understand by press reports that he was having the memorandum studied by a group of experts. Recently, in the month of January, a report was published that the Prime Minister had sent the Minister of Labour a letter requesting detailed answers to nineteen pertinent questions relating to Canada's man-power situation. The minister the other day verified that statement, but tried to laugh it off by saying that it was merely a routine matter. Was the letter ever sent? If so, what were the nineteen questions and what were the answers? I do not know, as a matter of fact, that the letter ever was sent, but it would be a matter of tremendous interest to the people of Canada if they could see the questions and the answers. So far we have had very little enlightenment from the administration. Some slight hint, I am bound to say, of the attitude of the ministry was given by the Prime Minister in this debate, when he intimated in veiled language that it was not easy to transfer labour from one branch of industry to another in this country. But apart from that we have been kept in the dark, and I do say that elucidation of this whole matter should be given to the Canadian people. It should be brought out into the light of day.
True, we have a new national war labour board under Mr. Justice McTague, and I pause here to say that in my view, so far as the chairman is concerned, the government could not have made a better selection. I am not quite so certain about the other gentlemen. I am going to reserve judgment until we see what their performance is. My own view and, I believe, the view of public opinion in this country, is that the government refuses to deal realistically with this problem, one of the great problems before the nation. It has adopted a policy of hedge and compromise, and that has emasculated the whole selective service plan.
I am indeed glad to see the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) in his place to-day, because I am concerned about the reinforcement position of our troops overseas.

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
For three years the Canadian army has been in training in the old land. It has not yet been in action. That is no fault of theirs. We are told that they are the best trained and equipped army in the world, and that is high praise. I hope it is true. I believe it is true in large measure, but the fact remains that they have not been in action, and when the testing time comes, as come it must, be it soon or late, this whole question of reinforcements for the fighting units of our army overseas becomes of paramount importance.
If the casualties are as high as they were at Dieppe, or even if they are half as high as they were at Dieppe, what is the position of reinforcements then? In the last war, I am assured, for every fighting man in the trenches it was the objective of the Canadian authorities to have one hundred per cent reinforcement man for man, so far as that was possible. That was the target aimed at; that was the objective. I do not say that it was always reached, but I am told by those who have knowledge of military matters that that should be'the ratio. What is the ratio to-day? We have never been told and we should be told. The information should be given.
There are certain- questions which I desire to put to the Minister of National Defence. I shall not expect him to answer them to-day or to-morrow. When the war appropriation bill is before the house I hope he will answer them fully, so that we, the people's representatives, may understand what the true position is. I believe it is in the national interest to put these questions to the minister, and that they should be answered, so that the house and the country may know exactly what the man-power situation is as it affects the armed forces.
In 1942 our army establishment consisted of an active army overseas, the home army, and the veterans' guard, and it was greatly increased in that year. We have now six divisions overseas and two in Canada-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Five.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I thought there were six. However, together they constitute a huge army for this little nation of eleven and a half million people. These are my questions:
1.	What is the total establishment for these divisions (a) in fighting men, (b) in auxiliary units?
2.	How is that establishment being maintained?
3.	How many men have been requisitioned during the last fourteen months, say since January 1, 1942?
4.	How many men have been actually received in the training centres in that period, (a) as volunteers for the active army overseas, and (b) draftees who have not volunteered?
5.	How many men have been returned from overseas and discharged from the army because of disabilities and unfitness since the first division went overseas? I fancy the number is rather large and I am surprised at it.
6.	What is the number and quality and extent of the training of the men. who are sent to replace them?
I may tell the minister frankly, I have heard some disquieting rumours about the character and quality of the training of men who have been sent overseas as reinforcements and additions to the troops. I have heard that some of them had not completed their four months' basic training. I know that if they are not put into action- at once they will complete their training in England, but I suggest that every man sent overseas in a reinforcement un-it should have at least his basic training in Canada if that be possible.
7.	Most important of all, what is the ratio of reinforcements or replacements, (a) overseas, and (b) in Canada, to -the number of fighting men in the divisions overseas?
8.	If the Canadian army goes into action in an invasion- of continental Europe, how long can the present ratio of reinforcements or replacements be maintained under the presen-t set-up?
9.	What is the present position of voluntary
enlistment?
10.	In the event of Canada's army being engaged in large-scale action in Europe or some other major theatre of war, cam its establishment on the present basis be maintained, at what rate and for how long?
These are searching questions. It is my conviction from what I have been told that if the Canadian army is engaged in any large scale action, say in an invasion of Europe, and the casualties are even half what they were at Dieppe, where I believe casualties and prisoners went as high as sixty-seven per cent, the ratio of reinforcements will be exhausted in a month. That may not be true, but I should like to know. If it be true, what then? It is our responsibility, I submit, to the men in the active army overseas, and to the people of Canada who are so magnificently supporting them, to get the facts and to be in a position to know and to urge upon the government appropriate action; for when the testing time comes these trained

I thank the house for its indulgence. I will not trespass too much on the good nature of the house in the days to come.
After three years Canada has done well in certain aspects of her war effort. I rather attribute that to the urgings and promptings and proddings that we gave to the government for three long years. I am proud of the little Royal Canadian Navy, even though it has not any capital ships. I know some of the personnel of that navy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They have sunk a good many submarines.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, I said I was proud of them, although they had not any capital ships. But you cannot run before you can walk, and you cannot walk before you creep. I am proud, very proud, of the contribution of the Royal Canadian Air Force. I think our greatest contribution in fighting capacity has been in the noble lads who have gone-I was going to say to every theatre of war-from the Royal Canadian Air .Force. I saw them in action myself in England, and I know something of the character and temper of the men who are operating day in and day out at great danger to themselves. The casualty lists that come to us daily tell a more eloquent tale of their heroism than any words I could summon to my assistance.
May I say to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) that Canada is now in her stride in production, and any meed of praise that is coming to him personally he can have from me. But the greatest praise should go to private industry-and by private industry I do not mean only executives and management; I mean for the most part executives, management and labour. There have been bottlenecks in production; I know of some of them. At times I have known of bottlenecks in the production of aircraft. I have never splashed it on the pages of the newspapers, but I have taken the opportunity to write occasionally to the director of aircraft

production, and he has been good enough to tell me of some of the troubles in connection with production.
I wish to deal briefly with this amendment of our socialist friends. I shall not read it, but I call attention to a phrase in the body of the proposed amendment in which the leader of that party refers to the powers contained in the National Resources Mobilization Act and their application to war industries and financial institutions "in the same manner" what is the significance of those words-"as they are being applied to the mobilization of man-power for military service"? If he means in the sense that men have been bludgeoned into the active army overseas under false pretenses, I am not in agreement; for I know some of the methods that have been employed to get men to enlist as "volunteers" in the days gone by. I wish before this debate is over he would elucidate just what he means by that phrase. I am at a loss to know what he does mean.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The meaning is obvious.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not think it is. The truth of the matter is that there is nothing new in this amendment to the amendment. It is in effect a repetition of the principles underlying the policy outlined by the leader of the socialist party at the last session. But behind the 'principle enunciated by that amendment is his proposal that in the first two years after the war is concluded the government of this country shall spend five billion dollars to provide against unemployment. I suggest that that proposal is wholly political, that it is looking for the votes of the people. He does not tell us how that money should be raised or to what it should be devoted. It is the most colossal bribe ever offered to the people of Canada. The intention is to bribe the people with their own money; that is what that proposal means, at all events to me. Therefore it is "wholly political.
Does the hon. gentleman think that government spending will cure unemployment? Let him look at recent history, not of this nation alone but also of Britain and the United States. It was tried in Britain and was condemned. Mr. Roosevelt tried it in the United States on a colossal scale, and it failed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

What did you do in
1932?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We tried it on a minor scale and it failed. It will never work; government spending can never under our economic system take the place of private enterprise. It can help.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
How would you do it, then?

The Address-Mr. Breithaupt

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wonder if the hon. member heard President Roosevelt last Friday night, when he stated unequivocally that private initiative and private enterprise would supply employment after the war, and that if it could not take up the full slack, then congress by legislation and otherwise would devise ways and means of taking up the slack. That is the attitude of the greatest national leader of the United States since the time of Lincoln. But government spending is not the cure for unemployment-and, by the way, neither is the Beveridge plan. They are mere palliatives. It is an aid to private enterprise and private initiative, but it is in no sense a substitute.	,
I suggest that under any democratic system private enterprise is the only effective agency that can give full employment, and you cannot have private employment under a system of controlled governmental regimentation such as my socialistic friends visualize. You cannot have a successful system of private enterprise unless it is a system of free enterprise, controlled, if you will, against abuse and exploitation, but free to engage in useful production with the aid of governmental action and supervision.

speechtext:
It has not failed. It has had its weaknesses; but your ipse dixit that it has failed does not prove that it has, and never will. Believing thoroughly in that system, I propose to vote against the subamendment.
Mr. L. 0. BREITHAUPT (Waterloo North): Mr. Speaker, I should like first to address a word of welcome to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) who is back in our midst to-day. All hon. members agree that he is a busy man. Sometimes we think he is too busy; certainly he does not consider his own physical welfare. From time to time he visits Kitchener, the city from which I come, but on those visits he moves so rapidly that one can scarcely see him for dust. Particularly is this so when he visits No. 3 training camp of the Canadian Women's Army Corps. His visits of inspection are always a source of inspiration.
In spite of the suggestion that all frills be eliminated from the debate, and that the usual congratulatory references to the mover and the seconder be dispensed with, nevertheless in view of the fact that this is my first speech from the floor of the house and that the mover and the seconder are members of the armed forces, I am sure that under the circumstances even the leader of the
opposition (Mr. Graydon) will excuse me if I transgress in this respect. Both the mover and the seconder are to be congratulated upon their splendid and eloquent addresses. I think it was most appropriate that two soldier members of parliament should have been selected to fill so ably this important assignment.
A personal note about the mover, the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris) will, I hope, be permitted. On his recent return from overseas the hon. member had as his cabin mate a near relative of mine who is a captain in the Scots Fusiliers of Canada. He had not had the pleasure of meeting the hon. member prior to that crossing. Reports he gave me upon his return to Kitchener respecting the good character and high ideals of the man he had the pleasure of meeting and with whom he bunked only serve to bear out the earlier impressions the hon. member for Grey-Bruce has already made upon all hon. members of the house. Undoubtedly similar favourable reports as to the character and high ideals of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Halle), who so ably seconded the motion, could be given by those from his native province who know him best.
Personally I am strongly convinced that the great body of men in the armed services who are fighting our battles should receive not only our unstinted praise and thanks for their great sacrifices, but as the opportunity presents itself should be further honoured by being placed in high positions in the government of our country. My suggestion in this connection is that Lieutenant-Colonel Merritt, V.C., of Dieppe fame, be named to. fill one of the existing vacancies in the upper house. Surely a man of his type would be a valuable acquisition to the parliament of Canada, particularly in the post-war period when men of his calibre and courage can contribute so much to the stabilization which will then be so necessary.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is noted for progressive innovations, such as the appointment of the first lady senator. Who can doubt his wise choice in this connection? I am sure he will not consider it out of place if I make a suggestion which I feel will be equally progressive and popular with the people of Canada. I trust he will give this matter his early and favourable consideration.
Just a word about the riding of Waterloo North, which I have the honour to represent. It is the historic constituency which first sent our present illustrious Prime Minister to the House of Commons. He was born in Kitchener and it was from his native city that he first

The Address-Mr. Breithaupt
came to Ottawa to represent the good people of that great industrial and agricultural riding. As a small boy I well remember his first vigorous campaign there. If you will permit me to say so, Mr. Speaker, election fights of those days had a far more interesting rough and tumble tone and a far greater interest was manifested on behalf of the voters in exercising their franchise, than campaigns of recent years in which the radio is so extensively-perhaps too extensively-used. In passing I cannot help contrasting the elections of yesteryear with those of to-day, particularly municipal elections in which there is an alarming lack of interest on the part of the voters in the exercise of their democratic rights. I am told that in a municipal election recently in Toronto less than twenty-five per cent of those entitled to vote took the trouble to go to the polls. This general matter was recently given careful study by the council of Kitchener, and recommendations were made to the various governments in this respect. It is to be hoped that some remedy for this apathetic trend will be found at an early day.
To come back to Waterloo North, may I tell the house how proud the people of his native town were to have had the honour of first sending to parliament their native son, our present Prime Minister, and how proud they still are of his grand record of achievement in the many years of unselfish service he has given to his country since that time. Their justifiable pride is enhanced by the fact that he has a longer record of government leadership than the head of any other allied nation. As he himself said in jest the other day, "Prince Albert now has the best of representation". I can assure you Mr. Speaker, in all earnestness, that this opinion is shared by the good people of Waterloo North, who heartily concur in this jocular observation. Undoubtedly as time goes on some move will be originated in the Prime Minister's native riding, in which I hope the whole of Canada will be privileged to assist, to recognize suitably the fact that it was there he was born and it was there he spent his boyhood days.
The riding from which I hail has been the battleground of many hard-fought campaigns. I cannot let this opportunity pass without also paying tribute to the splendid service rendered to his country by my immediate predecessor, the Hon. W. D. Euler, former minister of trade and commerce and now a member of the upper chamber. In the discharging of his duties in numerous portfolios of government there was not a more conscientious or able minister. Others who have preceded me were Mr. J. E. Seagram and

Mr. W. G. Weichel. It makes me very humble indeed and conscious of my great responsibility when I consider the men who have previously represented Waterloo North in this house.
Much has been said in this chamber during this debate about the plight of agriculture and the unhappy lot of the farmer in these strenuous war days. Fortunately the farmers in our district have developed mixed farming over the past years, to perhaps a far greater extent than in many other parts of the country, and therefore one perhaps does not see as much distress there as has arisen in other parts of Canada where a similar technique has not-been developed to the same extent. It is gratifying to note that with the much larger shipments of hogs, cattle and dairy products from the west, along with the higher prices received for them, mixed farming is developing rapidly and continued improvement can be looked for throughout the country.
I have recently been in touch with members of the wartime prices and trade board and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in connection with the butter fat subsidy being paid to the producers of dairy butter. I am pleased to be able to say that while this matter was overlooked in the original butter fat subsidy, it is now being considered. It is hoped that announcement will be made soon and the plight of these farmers overcome, particularly in view of the fact that under the coupon system the farmers would receive coupons when they sold their butter, which coupons could be used as a basis for settlement so far as the subsidy is concerned.
I notice in connection with the beef shortage that it has been announced recently that freight subsidies will be paid in connection with the shipment of western cattle to tire eastern market to relieve this shortage. These shipments will augment the supply of beef in the more thickly populated provinces of central Canada. This is an intelligent move and fine as far as it goes, but it appears to me from information I have gleaned from many farmer friends that this is only a palliative. They say that the beef shortage would be very quickly overcome if the price were set immediately at the May figure instead of registering periodical advances as the season progresses. Whether this will be done without puncturing the all-important price ceiling, I am not aware, but if it can be done I think it would be a tremendous relief so far as the beef situation is concerned.
Apart from any other benefits which would accrue, there are undoubtedly others worthy of consideration. First, shipments would be coming to the market before the ravages of

The Address-Mr. Breithaupt
the warble fly had reached peak proportions on winter stable-fed cattle. Second, the hides from these cattle would be freer from grub holes caused by the warble fly and as a result would be much superior to those hides taken off later in the season. They would produce leather and shoes much more suitable in quality for high-grade leather footwear for the armed forces. It is a well known fact that a serious hide shortage as well as a beef shortage is developing in this country, and unless steps are taken promptly to ensure a greater flow of cattle to the killing floors and an increase in imports, if necessary, of raw materials from South America, a situation will develop which will be most embarrassing so far as the providing of footwear to the armed forces is concerned.
While provisions have been made for postponement of military service for farmers and essential war workers, in the opinion of many these provisions did not go far enough. In order to ensure continuity of effort these postponements should be changed to exemptions, the future status to be changed only in case the present needs of the armed forces for farmers and war workers become more urgent than at present. By making this change our producers could plan a much better flow of war production than is now possible with farmers and war workers living in constant uncertainty.
I think most hon. members are interested in the controls and administrations that have been set up, and I would not be fair to the people of my constituency or to the people of Canada as a whole if I did not register their strong disapproval of some of the rulings of certain of the administrators who hold positions of war-time control. It is the general feeling that far too large a percentage of these temporary appointees are ruling with an iron hand and without consultation with those affected or with those who know the answers to their problems. They are entirely unmindful of the fact that in a democracy, for whose rights we are at present engaged in a life and death struggle, the people and their representatives are entirely disregarded and dealt with in a far too arbitrary manner.
Recently one of my constituents came to Ottawa to discuss a matter with one of the control officers. He was given a fair hearing but he was told that in no case would it further his cause to bring with him the representative of his constituency. I do not know whether other hon. members have had the same experience. None of us is looking for additional work in these strenuous days, but I do think that in matters in respect of which
the member can be of help to his constituency, he should be allowed to go to see a controller or administrator.
There are far too many examples which might be cited at this time, but the outstanding regulation concerning which one hears perhaps the most violent objections is the fifty-mile bus limit regulation. The unnecessary inconvenience caused to many passengers particularly those in the armed forces who are on leave and those in essential war industry, is in my opinion entirely unnecessary. If it is necessary to curtail further the use of gasoline and rubber, it has been suggested that the travelling schedules be amended by having fewer buses run, but let those which are running carry passengers to their destinations and eliminate the present practice of discharging them from the bus into snowdrifts or wherever they happen to be.
There is another matter which I think might very well be considered by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). It is a ruling which I believe has greatly impeded our war effort. I refer to the extreme restrictions on the taxicab business in Canada. It may be argued that these restrictions are necessary in view of the shortages, but I strongly maintain that this branch of transportation should be one of the last to suffer so extremely. Surely the services it renders are more important than those rendered by many other forms of transportation, and I would urge the minister to reconsider this matter so that at least the taxicab operators can increase their fares to a level commensurate with the additional costs and present hardships.
In the remarks made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) recently I was pleased to note his assurance to this house that appointees in the various control departments would in the future to a far greater extent than in the past be responsible for their actions to their ministers and to parliament as a whole. This is a very welcome announcement and one which will be received by the people of Canada as a necessary and constructive development. I believe that the large majority of Canadian citizens appreciate the splendid work and many personal sacrifices which most of these gentlemen are making, and if the few cases are dealt with as the Prime Minister has suggested I think all reasons for complaint on this score will be quickly removed.
I want to say a word about the civil service. I think it is only proper that at this time we should pay high tribute to the civil service as a whole. I have come in contact
The Address-Mr. Breithaupt

with a great many members of the civil service, both here and in my travels throughout the country, and have noted not only that they are faithful in discharging their regular peace-time duties but that many of them, motivated by high patriotic principles of service, have willingly undertaken additional responsibilities. They are doing a splendid job, and many of them are discharging duties far beyond those of their original positions. But I think the time has come when we should not only pay tribute to the civil service but see that they are paid a proper remuneration for the work they are doing. Many of the civil service do not receive the cost of living bonus. These are matters which might be very carefully considered so that the civil service can get a much better break.	.
Coming to the speech from the throne, I see much in it to commend itself to the people of Canada. I cannot agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) that it is an indefinite document. Personally I think it is clear and terse. It leaves no doubt as to what it means with respect to the various policies it mentions. I am pleased to note that it forecasts a further expansion of the Royal Canadian Navy. The remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury with respect to the Royal Canadian Navy may be considered, I think, as damning it with faint praise, but he tried to make up for that by saying later on that the navy had done a good job. In my observation, Mr. Speaker, the Royal Canadian Navy has done a splendid job under the veiy able leadership of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services tMr. Macdonald). Undoubtedly the submarine menace is the greatest we have now to contend with. I believe that the navy and the merchant marine should be increased to the greatest possible extent so that we may have more and more ships not only to transport war supplies but to protect our own shores, and let us have these ships without delay.
The speech from the throne states also that parliament is to be asked to make further grants towards Canada's making her utmost contribution to the winning of the war. These are desirable and necessary, and no doubt will be cheerfully agreed to by all parties in this house.
I am also pleased to note, in spite of what the hon. member for York-Sunbury has said, that the government is making further efforts to economize in other directions wherever economies are possible. Buildings and tracts of land temporarily required by the services should in my opinion in future be rented

and not purchased. I am convinced that both large and small economies can still be effected which would ease considerably the lot of the overburdened taxpayer. I do not see the sense in purchasing many buildings for the different departments if we can get along by renting buildings. This trend towards buying new buildings should be carefully considered, and buildings should only be purchased where it is absolutely necessary to do so.
In a conversation recently with me the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) indicated that there was far too great a tendency for many departments of the government to place their financial requirements on his doorstep, on the assumption that they could readily and easily be taken care of. While the Minister of Finance and his capable aides have done a splendid job in achieving their various financial objectives, nevertheless I believe that their burdens in this connection should be eased to the greatest possible extent. The Minister of Finance is doing a splendid job and it is up to every spending body in the government and to every member of this house to support his efforts and those of his aides. I am convinced that if the spending departments not directly connected with the war effort will continue' to make strenuous efforts to cut down unnecessary expenditures the tax burden will be very materially lightened.
I want to say a word about the pay-as-you-go income tax plan. I am glad to see that the speech from the throne contains the forecast that further measures will be introduced to alleviate the present situation in regard to outstanding income taxes accumulated from previous years. This announcement has been well received by all classes of the community. I have received a great many petitions from working people in my riding who to a man are favourable to having this change made in collecting the income tax. It is to be hoped that when legislation is brought down dealing with this matter no discrimination will be shown and that all taxpayers will receive the same treatment. I hope that the legislation will provide for complete cancellation of back taxes.
While I am on the subject of finance I wish to make a suggestion to the minister, and that is that when the new budget comes before us for consideration provision will be made for returning to the former method of collecting income taxes from employees through what was known as the national defence tax plan. I think some similar plan should be adopted now, because the present system is too complicated and too cumbersome, particularly for

The Address-Mr. Dorion
workers who are not accustomed to keeping books and accounts. I submit that a straight deduction in the form of the old defence tax, instead of the present complicated method, would materially reduce the serious trend towards absenteeism in essential industry, and that a greater incentive to stay on the job would accrue to the worker.
I cannot let this opportunity pass, Mr. Speaker, without congratulating the Minister of Finance and his able assistants upon the policies adopted by this government for price control and controlling inflation. That the policy pioneered by this government has been remarkably effective is indicated by the fact that from November 1, 1941, the high point prior to the imposition of the price ceiling, to December 1, 1942, the official cost-of-living index in this country has risen by a little more than two per cent, while in the United States, where controls have not been as effective as here, the corresponding increase has been nearly ten per cent. Compare this truly remarkable record with conditions that existed in the last war. The Canadian cost of living then rose in a similar period by more than twenty per cent. While one hears many fair and unfair criticisms of the government, it is regrettable that one hears so little of an achievement in price control which is truly outstanding, not only in Canada but in other countries, none of which has been able to surpass Canada's record, let alone equal it.
Just a word, in closing, about social security. The. indication in the speech from the throne that a select committee from the house will soon be appointed to examine and report on questions of social and health insurance is timely, highly desirable and has met with public approval. I feel, however, that timely and desirable as these all-important objectives are, the winning of the war and the defeat of the axis powers with the utmost dispatch is still objective number one, and must be pursued with relentless determination. But I wish to congratulate the government upon having taken the initial steps to bring about a greater measure of social security for the people of Canada in the post-war period. This government has done much in the past to improve living conditions through progressive- I might say liberal progressive-legislation, such as unemployment insurance and other similar acts. And now, by the introduction of legislation which will provide in the final analysis a still greater measure of freedom from fear and want than has ever been experienced in the history of the country, it has shown its direct interest in and its ability to deal with such all-important subjects affecting the everyday life of our people, and at the
same time to foster free enterprise and individual initiative. I am sure that such a measure will be well received by the people of our great country who share with me the basic belief that Canada, having demonstrated clearly through her production record in this all-out war effort and through the energy and resourcefulness of her people, that she can carry on and finance successfully, by the same token should be able in peace time to plan and produce so that all her citizens shall have the right to employment and to a share in the heritage to which they are so justly entitled.

speechtext:
My first words in this house are words of thanks: thanks to you, Mr. Speaker, for the kindness you have shown me since I have been here; thanks to the hon. members of this house whom I have had the privilege of meeting in the course of the last two weeks, for their hearty welcome; thanks especially to the hon. members for Gaspe (Mr. Roy), Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe), who dared to come and help me during my recent electoral campaign; but thanks over and above all to the electors of Charlevoix-Saguenay for the magnificent support which they gave me on the 30th of November last.
I wonder whether all hon. members have a true knowledge of the constituency which I have the honour to represent. May I be allowed to give a short description of it so as to complete if necessary the information they already have?
If we look at the map we can see that it is the largest constituency in the dominion. It starts from Chateau Richer, a place situated fifteen miles below Quebec on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, and it goes as far as Labrador, over eight hundred miles farther. It encloses all the northern part of the province of Quebec from the St. Lawrence to Hudson bay and Hudson strait.
I must tell the house that this very large area of our country has not yet been developed as it should have been, owing to lack of means of communication. In the western part, that is to say west of the Saguenay river, we have roads, and one railroad which goes as far as Murray Bay. In the eastern part, east of the Saguenay river, which is the larger area, we have just one road about a hundred miles long, as far as Comeau bay, and beyond that we have only the water and the air as means of communication.
I know, Mr. Speaker, having been informed by experts, that our country possesses great natural resources. There are huge water powers,
The Address-Mr. Dorion

rich mines, wonderful forests, and in numerous places the soil can be cultivated to great advantage. The best and probably the only way to provide this country with the necessaiy means of development would be to build a road along the north shore of the St. Lawrence. In this regard I wish to draw the attention of the government to the fact that the building of such a road would be very useful for the defence of our country and for the help of our allies; in fact it could be used to carry food and war materials to the Atlantic coast and to Newfoundland. Would it not be the safest way to provide the eastern military stations with the necessary equipment, food and war materials?
Furthermore, this road, which would be very useful for military purposes during the war, would also be immensely advantageous after the war. It does not happen very often that we have the opportunity of undertaking military works which will become necessary improvements after the war. The building of this road is one of them. That is why I urge upon the government that they consider this'project and execute it as soon as possible.
Now, Mr. Speaker, allow me to tell you that this constituency is inhabited by over 65,000 right-minded and peaceful people whose only desire is to devote themselves to their country and their families. They love this country which has been built up by their forefathers and to which they are loyal. They like the democratic system under which we are living and they want to keep it. They have fought in the past for the maintenance of their rights, their creed and their tongue, and having been successful in preserving them, having no attachment to any other part of the world, they are deeply rooted to the soil out of which they themselves, like their forefathers, have extracted their living, and they are not much interested in international disputes. They understand, however, that we are now fighting for the safeguarding of democracy, and they are willing to share the war effort in so far as it does not annihilate altogether their national patrimony. They believe that the right definition of democracy has been given by Lincoln, as follows:
Government of the people, by the people, for the people.
They believe also that, as was expressed by Mr. H. E. Manning, K.C., a few months ago:
The essence of democracy is respect for the rights of minorities. In their contempt for the rights of minorities lies the iniquity of totalitarian systems. Beware lest in the heat and stress of war we trample upon the rights of

minorities. If we do we shall have cast away the thing for which lives are being sacrificed and fortunes squandered.
We believe also that if our efforts to-day must be directed towards the winning of the war, we must not forget that we have to prepare for the post-war period. The publication of the Beveridge report containing a programme for social security in Great Britain has aroused world-wide interest. In the United States the national resources planning board has placed a somewhat similar programme before President Roosevelt, calling for extension of social security measures. The technical adviser of the board, Mr. W. J. Cohen, recently said, commenting on the Beveridge report:
If Great Britain during her life and death struggle can find the time to undertake during the course of the war a comprehensive evaluation of her whole social security system, then surely we can follow a similar course. It is becoming increasingly clear that an extended social security programme is as necessary to victory as is production of guns and ships.
The people of Charlevoix-Saguenay, like the people of the whole province of Quebec, desire earnestly the establishment of a true national unity throughout Canada, unity not only in words, 'but in facts, unity not only in war time but also in peace time. They want to remain what their fathers were at the time of the building of the confederation, that is to say, the partners of their English fellow citizens, and not their inferiors. They want to do their utmost to attain the object our fathers had in mind, the building of a great nation.
On this point, may I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to tell this house that we in Canada must at last attain our unity not in regimentation, but in a balanced, well-knit cooperative diversity. Otherwise our historic and present mission will not be fulfilled. Lord Tweedsmuir said five years ago:
Canada can never be quite like her neighbour, and that is all to the good; for it means that she has a specific contribution of her own to make to North American civilization. I like to think of her, with her English and French peoples, as in a special degree the guardian of the great Mediterranean tradition which descends from Greece and Rome, and which she has to mould to the uses of a new world. I want to see her keep her individuality; for that is of inestimable advantage, not only to her, but to her neighbour.
If we, the members of this parliament, followed these wise admonitions, I am sure we would contribute to the settlement of many internal misunderstandings.
We must not forget, either, that we are here to participate, as representatives of the people, in the government of this country. But,

The Address-Mr. Dorion
looking around me, since I have been here, and trying to find out what we had to do, I came to the conclusion that most of our privileges had been vested in numerous boards and commissions. We have built up an enormous bureaucracy; we have administrators of every conceivable trade appointed by the wartime prices and trade board; we have controllers of every kind. We have different boards and different administrators giving conflicting orders and conducting duplicated and triplicated investigations of the same thing, and we have an immense amount of red tape. What is worse, many of these administrators and controllers are young men without experience, and are the real makers of the laws of this country.
Think of it just a moment, and see if it is fair and reasonable that our whole economic system should be in the hands of these dictators. The people of this country are not satisfied with this state of things, and the government should bring in the necessary corrections.	[DOT]
Even if our efforts and our energies must be directed towards the winning of the war, we must not forget that we shall have to live again in this country after the war. We must, if our political system has failed to bring us all the satisfaction we wanted, do our utmost to improve the situation. This is the reason why, in September 1941, at the suggestion of the hon. member for Gaspe, a few hundred people, from all parts of the province of Quebec and from all ranks of society, met in Quebec and adopted the following resolution:
This meeting expresses the wish that the efforts of the people of Canada in this war be rewarded with success; and this gathering prays the Almighty to stand by our armies and those of our allies in order that a definite victory be achieved.
Our country will then enjoy a lasting peace which will favour the full development of the vital forces of the various technical groups and will foster an intimate collaboration among them, this to be achieved in a spirit of constitutional liberty and social justice; thus paying the way to the creation of a truly and exclusively Canadian nation.
This resolution contains a real programme which could and should be accepted by all true Canadians.
Before closing my remarks in English, I cannot refrain from referring to a declaration made the other day by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), which was reproduced in big headlines by some newspapers. He was referring to the sinking of enemy submarines by Canadian corvettes. Addressing himself to members sitting in this 72537-30
comer of the house he was asking us if we were not proud that a corvette manned by Canadians and bearing the name of the city of Quebec was able to sink an enemy ship on the waters of the Mediterranean. As this argument did not press upon me very strongly, I really could not prevent myself from smiling. It was then that the Prime Minister added:
Yet at this critical time, of all times, hon. gentlemen in the far corner opposite find it necessary to separate themselves from colleagues in their province in order to support an isolationist view with regard to the war effort of Canada! Their action does credit neither to themselves, nor to their province or to our country.
I thought at the time he was addressing himself to the hon. members sitting to my left, but the following day I noticed in the papers that my name was connected with those of the members for Beauharnois-Laprairie and for Beauce, and therefore that the public was under the impression that I too was pointed at as supporting an isolationist view.
I must state, first, that I am not associated with the hon. members who recently formed this new political group called Le Bloc Populaire, and I have not to come to their defence. But speaking for myself I wish to say that I have no lesson of loyalty to receive from anybody, because during the last war, instead of travelling through the United States, I enlisted at the age of nineteen in the Royal Air Force. I went and served overseas and I came back with my commission of lieutenant in the imperial army. To-day my only son, who is twenty years of age, student at law at Laval university, voluntarily enlisted two years ago in the Canadian Officers' Training Corps. I think that settles the question.
Furthermore I found it very peculiar to hear the Prime Minister speak about isolationists. I wondered whether he did not remember what he and his colleagues had been telling the people of the province of Quebec during the last twenty-five years. I do not hesitate to declare that considering the attitude taken by the Liberal party during this period of time, no member of this party has the right to accuse anyone from the province of Quebec of being an isolationist.
(Translation)': Mr. Speaker, even if I could speak English as readily as French, I would make it my duty, on the occasion of my first speech in the house, to say in French what I have to add to my previous remarks, in order to stress the officially bilingual character of the house.
A few moments ago, I enumerated the reasons why the electors of Charlevoix-

45S
The Address-Mr. Dorion

Saguenay have put their trust in me, on November 30 last, and I wish to complete this statement.
First, my election constitutes an evident proof that the citizens of the province of Quebec refuse to support either of the two older parties. After forsaking the Conservative party, they long held to the hope that the Liberal party would guarantee the accomplishment of their legitimate yearnings. They honestly and loyally put their trust in the leaders of the Liberal party in their province of Quebec, who strongly condemned the Conservative external policy and promised that a just and fair solution would be found to the internal problems; they now realize to what extent they have been deceived.
After having, for 75 years, been tossed between "reds" and "blues" with the only result of serving as stepping stones to power, and without any advantage to themselves, they have become wary and, although not sure of the political orientation they will ultimately adopt, they have decided, for the present, to support men, who, having broken with old ties, can offer them guarantees of sincerity and above all, unselfishness.
If the citizens of the province of Quebec have reached this point, which I may call a strategic turn in their political history, it is because they have understood that their representatives in the past had been but a minority in both old parties and had been incapable of upholding their interests and, unfortunately, too often unequal to the task.
The French Canadians intend to play the part assigned to them in both political fields of the country. In the dominion field they want the spirit of the confederation pact maintained. They' ask for no more, but they are insistent on this point.
Is there, in this whole country, a single man who-could honestly claim that in the dominion government, the French Canadians get their rightful share? And is not this truer than ever since we have resorted to be governed by commissions? Let us review the list of these dictators who presently control the economic life of Canada, without any responsibility to the people through their representatives, and let us examine whether the French Canadian element gets its rightful share.
I do not claim that the solution of this problem lies in the granting to French Canadians of a few positions in the civil service or in the various dominion departments. This matter goes much deeper.
What is needed is that, through actual and active sharing of responsibilities by French Canadians in the government of the country,

our whole economic set-up should show plain evidences of the dual character of our institutions rendered necessary by the two racial elements making up the Canadian nation.
They want the representation in this house to be proportionate to the populations of the various provinces, as provided by the confederation pact. In my opinion, the government should, at this session, introduce a bill to effect such a redistribution of the electoral seats. Otherwise, we shall once again tear up another section of the confederation pact.
They claim that Canada, in its international relations, should be guided solely by the interests of its inhabitants; not as has so often been the case in the last 50 years, by the interests of some other nation.
They realize that Canada is an American country and that as long as its leaders endeavour to manage its international affairs as though it were European, they will never attain the object intended by the Fathers of Confederation.
They also claim that Canada should assume its proper place in the Pan-American Union and thereby reap all the privileges enuring from association with natural allies.
Indeed, whether we want it or not, in spite of the ready communications, which have lately brought all the nations of the world so much closer together, it remains true, nevertheless, that on each side of the Americas, there are oceans which will always have to be reckoned with, especially when we consider that, at the start of the present war, a 20-milewide channel has been enough to halt the ravaging hordes of the German dictator.
In the same train of thought, I take this opportunity to state that we are wondering why we are still allowed to have our legal problems solved by the Privy Council in London. The right of appeal to the Privy Council constitutes, in my way of thinking, a vestige of the former domination of the mother country over her colonies and I feel that this right of appeal should be abolished.
In the provincial field, I repeat what I said a few moments ago: all that the French Canadians want is the enforcement of the confederation pact. Unfortunately, jurists and politicians have not always been of a mind as to the proper interpretation of the British North America Act. respecting the relations between the provinces and the central government.
Two theories have been vigorously upheld. There are some who claim that the central government has precedence over the provincial administrations; they take the view that the confederation act is an act passed by the

The Address-Mr. Dorion
Imperial government and accepted by the contracting parties; the others say that it is a contract based on an agreement concluded by the provinces in 1867. This last theory has been brilliantly defended by a number of legal and political lights; it has even been accepted, in a certain measure, by the courts of law, at different times.
In the course of an enquiry held by a parliamentary committee, in 1935, to consider ways and means of amending the constitution, certain opinions have been expressed from which I shall quote the following extracts:
Hon. Mr. Veniot: Confederation is not based entirely on the Quebec resolutions.-
Mr. W. S. Edwards (Deputy Minister of Justice): I know.
Hon. Mr. Veniot: Because the Quebec resolutions make provision for certain jurisdiction on the part of the provinces which at the time of confederation when the act was passed in Great Britain were not included; for instance, jurisdiction with regard to immigration, and certain other matters such as fisheries were given to the provinces by the Quebec resolutions. When the Act of Confederation passed these were transferred to the dominion; and further than that, it must be understood I maintain that it was a strict agreement between the provinces.-
And Mr. Edwards added:
I agree with you, that it was an agreement.
Although I believe that the right of appeal to the Privy Council should be abolished, I am evidently not questioning the ability of the legal gentlemen sitting on that court. So that I have no hesitation in seeking a solution for our outstanding problems of the moment in the opinions which they have expressed. In this manner I have found in the rulings of the Privy Council arguments in favour of this second proposition regarding relations between central and provincial authorities.
In the case of John Deere Plow Co. versus Wharton there is mention by the Privy Council of a political agreement.
In the reference of the Initiative and Referendum Act, the Privy Council states that the constitution of Canada was adopted in 1867 by the Imperial Parliament in order to give effect to the wishes expressed in the resolutions adopted at the Conference of Canadians held at Quebec in October, 1864.
In the case of Edwards versus Attorney General for Canada, the Privy Council, referring to the B.NA. act, mentions that it is a case of compromise.
Again, in the reference concerning Regulation and Control of Aeronautics in Canada, the Privy Council once more mentions a political compromise.
Another theory has been put forth in recent years, known as the theory of Institution, and 72537-301
here is what an eminent Dominican sociologist, Reverend Father Delos, has to say about the definition given by Georges Renard:
An institution, says he, is the result of a communion of men in an idea, it constitutes the body, the reality, the being born of this communion. An idea to be realized, a purpose, "establishing solidarity between them who entertain it together or successively"; a community of purpose arising between contemporaries and successive generations. An institution, again according to Mr. Renard. is an idea supported by appropriate ways and means of eventual establishment, of realization, through the assumption of shape and objective being. . . . It entails the giving of an internal statute and organisms permitting external action, a coming into being as a social body enjoying internal life and external activity.
This doctrine has been upheld by men whose functions afforded them more than most others opportunities for a close study of the mechanism of the British North America Act. I would quote the opinion given by a journalist, Mr. Leopold Richer, which is to be found on page 125 of "Notre probleme politique''-.
We regret that up to tiie present our jurists should have offered commentaries on our national constitution which on the whole are rather superficial, oftentimes even of a controversial nature. It is not sufficient to state that our constitution is a legislative act; its nature, its finality and its origin must also be accurately defined. Nor is it sufficient to contend that the British North America Act does or does not constitute a contract or to dispose of the matter in a few pages.
But, for practical purposes, I am convinced that we are bound to conclude that the Canadian confederation was established, following an agreement between the various provinces and that, consequently, we must always consider the legitimate aspirations of each group forming the constituent elements of the dominion.
Although each province is interested in safeguarding its rights and privileges as conferred by the British North America Act, for the province of Quebec it is of essential and paramount importance. As a matter of fact, the history of the province of Quebec begins 100 years before that of the other provinces. We cherish special traditions; our culture does not spring from the same sources and our civil Law differs from that of the other provinces. We have, therefore, a very special ethnical character and that is why the citizens of Quebec are so anxious to safeguard the autonomy of their province at all costs, so that they may keep what they cherish above all else and thus avoid, in another field, useless arguments and dissensions.
The Address-Mr. Dorion

Unfortunately, in the last few years, and especially since the beginning of the; war, this provincial autonomy has been severely assailed.
Under the urgency of war, the dominion government has passed a number of laws curtailing the activities of the provinces to a large extent. We are often told that this centralizing policy is of a temporary character only; however, I must frankly admit that, this statement, in itself, does not constitute, in my opinion, a sufficient guarantee of an eventual return to normal conditions at the close of the war.
For these various reasons, the citizens of the province of Quebec, fearing, more than ever, that their provincial autonomy might disappear, are averse to supporting the old political parties who have both, each in its turn, shown tendencies toward centralization.
Once more, I say that they wish to cooperate with their English-speaking fellow-citizens. They are ready, as they were in 1867, to extend to them a loyal offer of cooperation in the erection of a great nation. They claim, with 'reason., that cooperation between the various elements of our population, when properly understood, does not mean assimilation, but the very opposite.
In conclusion, I ask my English-speaking fellow-citizens not to judge the ideals actuating the citizens of Quebec from reports that are too often fantastic. I believe these ideals are perfectly and briefly described in the following few sentences taken from the concluding remarks of a lecture given by Father Lionel Groulx, at the Monument National, in Montreal, on September 16, 1942:
Let us re-create our economic, political and national solidarity. Yes, doubtless, we form only a small, a very small people. We are reminded of this fact often enough, at the present time, when we are ceaselessly told that minorities have to submit to the harsh rule of majorities. But we know that, in the eyes of God, nations are not valued by their material, political or military strength, but by the nobility of their souls. And our faith, as well as our history, teach us that, in heaven, there is a merciful and generous Providence for the small nations who have the strength to accomplish their mission.
