speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few remarks this afternoon I wish first to associate myself with hon. members who have extended hearty and well deserved congratulations to the mover (Mr. Harris) and the seconder (Mr. Halle) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The efforts of these hon. members was an outstanding example of having the right men in the right place, saying the right things. Those hon. members not
*Mr. Dorion.]
only represent vital civilian communities in the dominion, but are representative of the Canadian forces who to-day in the different theatres of war are fighting for liberty.
I do not wish to trespass upon the time of the house by going into any detailed description of the commendable progress made by the Canadian people in their war effort. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and many other hon. members in their speeches have given factual and detailed analyses of our war effort. I am sure every hon. member and each intelligent person across the country knows the history of our successful programme, and I am equally sure each is proud of it. It is an achievement whereby, in four short years, Canada has been transformed from a state of military unpreparedness to the third greatest arsenal of the world. Not only is this a splendid achievement by the people of Canada, but it stands as a lesson to the whole world, because it reveals that we must have had first-class management by the ministers in charge of our war programme. Our war effort has given evidence of Canada's unlimited resources, and has shown the willingness and ability of our people to utilize our resources for the nation's good.
If we wrere to accept what we read in some parts of the press, and what we hear in some speeches both in and out of the house, we would think there was much disunity in Canada in connection with the carrying out of our war effort. I believe if we survey the facts any such idea will be driven from our minds. We will find that in every province of Canada thousands of our young men have enlisted voluntarily and have shown their willingness to serve in any theatre of war. Then, we must not forget the part played by our brave women,'some of whom have left lucrative secretarial and clerical positions in order to enter industrial plants for the purpose of releasing young men for the armed forces. Then, comparatively old men, men beyond middle age, men who experienced the hardships and horrors of the last war, are voluntarily standing in arms to defend our shores. Men and women are giving freely and generously, not only of their savings but of their earnings. These offerings amounting to huge sums are given to assist Canada in her gigantic war effort. We find to-day that the taxpayers are accepting without murmur the burdens which are placed upon them by way of taxation and which, as the war goes on, will become greater and greater. We find that our people are not complaining about the restrictions and rationing which are im-

The Address-Mr. McGarry
portant elements in our war effort. To-day the housewife is obliged to accept inferior substitutes for commodities which were available in peace time. She has had to deny herself the use of certain utensils which would make her work easier and more expeditious.
The travel of business men and pleasure seekers has been reduced to the minimum, but we hear very little murmuring about this. In many instances the present volume of business of industrial employers is only a fraction of what it was prior to the war. Many of these men-there are some in my constituency- have been obliged to fold up but we hear very little complaining.
Does this indicate disunity? What does this generosity, this tolerance, and this willingness to pay indicate? Does it not reveal that our people are intelligent and that they realize that the winning of the war is the all-important thing? Does it not reveal that they realize that their money would be no good if we were overrun by the hun? They realize that the sacrifices and inconveniences which they are suffering to-day are as nought compared with the serfdom, tyranny and butchery to which they would be subjected if our allied forces did not succeed in turning back those who would be world dominators. All these things show clearly that our people are united, and show that they are capable of cooperating with the other powers to carry on this great effort. I believe that when the history of the world is written one thing that will stand out among the records of all countries is that in proportion to population Canada has contributed more to this war effort than any of our allies.
We hear sometimes that there is a lack of preparedness for the aftermath of this war. I believe, and I imagine almost every Canadian believes, that while the successful prosecution of this war should be uppermost in our minds, we must have some thought for the day when the thousands of men and women now employed in industrial work revert to their peacetime pursuits. There must be some planning for that time. Prices will drop from the dizzy heights of war time down to the lower and stable levels of peace time. We must plan if we are going to avoid the terrible depression which we experienced after the last war, some of the pangs of which were almost as bad as anything we have experienced during this war and many of the results of which have not entirely disappeared.
Has our government taken any notice of this? What do we find? Three months after war was declared in 1939 this government established the wartime prices and trade board.
We all know the effect of that. As a result of the control there has been over prices we are not looking to-day on the disgraceful spectacle we witnessed in the last war when men grew fat on the sacrifices and blood of the nation. The government has been doing a little planning all along. Take, for instance, the land settlement act. We all know what a failure the former act was. It was nothing more or less than a racket, but under the amendment, which is remedial in character, security is now accorded to the settler and he knows that he will be sustained on his land. The present regulations provide that the land must be up to a certain standard of production and that the man who goes on the land must have some experience as a farmer. In fact, it does the very thing the old scheme failed to do, namely, put the right man on the right farm.
There are also the' compulsory reemployment regulations. These were introduced by the government during the last war. It may be difficult to figure out just how effective they will be in the solution of the unemployment problem, but they will help to solve that problem. There is also the Unemployment Insurance Act, a remedial measure to provide for our unemployed. Without doubt the coffers will be full after this war is over, and at least some temporary relief will be provided for the unemployment situation.
All these things go to show that the government has been planning from the inception of the war for the aftermath of the war. We who have faith in our Prime Minister, we who have faith in our government are happy to learn of this splendid forecast of future planning. We hear a great deal about planning for the future and about planning for social and economic security. In the flood of literature which the post-war economic problem has engendered there is some that is constructive and far-reaching in scope, but if we examine it all closely we find that much of it is doctrinaire and speculative.
If we are going to talk about economic security we should know what it means. There is a great difference, and we must differentiate between what is government regulation and what is cramping and regimentation. Judicious regulation is splendid, but rigid regimentation which cramps and stultifies is quite different, and I would say that the government in taking charge of matters which will be conducive to economic security had better limit itself to doing the things that private enterprise cannot do and leave private enterprise free to do what the government itself cannot do. There is no doubt, and I think we have a good example of it in our own government, that a government can create
The Address-Mr. McGarry

an environment in which economic progress can be accelerated; but, on the other hand, regimentation stultifies the whole process of economy. What we want is a balance between the two; and if ever we needed a balance in this Canada of ours, if ever it was needed in this world, it is now when the ship of state is riding on such a stormy sea. I have every confidence that the government, which has carried on its war programme in such a splendid and commendable way and made such a success of it, even while planning for the problems of the post-war period, will see to it that in its planning for social and economic security a proper balance will be maintained between government enterprise and private enterprise. I have every faith that after this "red" reign is over, our democracies will become much stronger as a result of their common experience, and that when they enter the council chamber of the world Canada will take a prominent part and will cooperate with her allies in regard to peace measures just as splendidly as she has cooperated with them in the prosecution of the war to victory.
I do not wish to be considered too regional, but I have a few local matters which I wish to submit to the government, and I will cite them now so that if the ministers directly concerned are not at the moment in the house they will be able to read my remarks in Hansard. On several occasions I have brought these local matters to the attention of the various ministers.
First, I would ask the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) to consider a matter which I have brought to his attention before. I refer to the establishment of an airport in the vicinity of Port Hawkesbury. We have there a large tract of land, and the topography and soil make it in every way suitable for an air base. It is on the direct route of the Trans-Canada airway. In the last couple of months there have been incidents which might cause the minister to look upon this suggestion favourably. Within one month four planes have crashed in that neighbourhood, and on each occasion the planes hoverpd over that area attempting to find a landing place. An emergency landing field at Port Hawkesbury not only would be of benefit to war planes, but after the war would be a splendid emergency landing field for commercial planes.
I would ask the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) to consider seriously the establishment of a naval port at Port Hawkesbury in the strait of Canso. I have before me a resolution from the town of Port Hawkesbury pointing out what must appeal at least to the Minister

of National Defence for Naval Services. The whereases in the resolution are as follows:
1.	Our harbour is such that ships of all sizes are afforded safe anchorage.
2.	The property already surveyed has already a sea wall established which gives a sufficient frontage and depth of water that will enable ships to lay to in safety.
3.	Railway facilities adjoin the property, a siding being already established.
4.	Fresh water for supplying ships easily available from an artesian w'ell already established.
5.	Gas, fuel oil as well as aviation gas storage tanks also established near the property operated by the Imperial Oil Company.
6.	Grounds surrounding site could easily be made available for drill, etc.
7.	Marine railway with machine shop available here which should be of priceless value during the present crisis.
8.	The serious economic situation prevailing in our county and considering the fact that no benefits have accrued on account of war activities should, we think, be a deciding factor.
9.	We as a committee offer our services in any way we could be of assistance in helping during these trying times.
10.	The old-established firm of boat builders is situated close by, where any necessary repairs could be effected.
We submit these facts with the hope that your decision will result in our having established here a base that will be practicable from every point of view.
I have on several occasions spoken to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) about the development of a magnetic iron ore deposit in the district of Glencoe in my constituency, and I would again ask him now to give this matter a little more consideration. We have also a deposit of tungsten in the northeastern end of Mar-garee district. I hope the house will pardon me for trespassing on its time in bringing these matters to the attention of the various ministers, but it is difficult at times to consult them in their offices. I would ask them to give these projects further consideration because I believe they would all be of great value in our war effort and, further, I think some recognition should be given of the splendid contribution which has been made to the war effort by the people of my constituency who, proportionately, have contributed as much as, if not more than, the people of any other constituency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to congratulate the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) upon the splendid recovery he has made from his recent serious accident. I am sure it is a great testimony to the skilful services which he has received from members of my profession in the city of Ottawa.

The Address-Mr. Bruce
May I also congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon his selection of a distinguished soldier to fill the position of Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleche).
The minister has made a number of patriotic speeches which have appealed to a large number of Canadians and with which I am personally heartily in accord. I am sure he will bring to this house a great deal of valuable assistance in the carrying out of our work.
I was pleased to note in the speech from the throne that some form of health insurance is forecast to be dealt with during the present session. It will be recalled by many hon. members that on several occasions during 1941 and 1942 I brought in an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act with the object of securing information upon which the government could base a national health insurance bill. I believe they have benefited by the suggestions I made, in that they have gathered a great deal of information which I understand is now ready to be presented to the select committee which has been appointed, and from which I hope a suitable measure of health insurance will emerge.
Might I recall to the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham) the circumstances under which that great statesman Sir John A. Macdonald adopted the name "Progressive Conservative." There were in Upper Canada the High Tories, under Sir Allan Napier MacNab, and the Moderate Conservatives under Mr. Macdonald; and then there were the Moderates and the Clear Grits. The Clear Grits were so called by their leader Mr. George Brown because, he said, they were all sand and no dirt-clear giit all the way through. The continual uncertainty of government with so many parties led Sir John Macdonald, on February 9, 1854, to attempt an enlargement of his party, when he stated:
Our aim should be to enlarge the bounds of our party so as to embrace every person desirous of being counted as a Progressive Conservative.
He succeeded speedily in his objective. Almost the only opposition in Upper Canada was from George Brown's Clear Grits, who later on changed their name to the "Reform" party; but a few of that party were dissatisfied with Mr. Brown, and they became the Baldwin Reformers, and ultimately emerged the Liberals. To-day we have the Hepburn Liberals and the King Liberals, and in this house we have been watching the gradual disintegration of the Liberal party. The first to break away was the Canada party in the southeast corner, formed by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe).
Then there was formed the Bloc Populaire, headed by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond). There is still a rump of this party who have not as yet crossed the floor of the house but who broke away from the Prime Minister on Bill No. 80 of last session, to amend the National Mobilization Resources Act, 1940. Then there is the group of some forty Liberals led by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), to whom the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) referred this afternoon. We are not quite certain as to the present position of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres. Is he still a follower of the Prime Minister or not, and where do these other forty men who joined him stand now?
According to the Prime Minister, however, the Progressive Conservatives have still another crime to answer for, namely, that of having frequently changed our leader. I say to him that this is the best proof that we are a truly democratic party, whereas the only way in which the members of his party can register their dissatisfaction with his leadership is by breaking away and forming the new groups to which I have just referred.
May I remind the Prime Minister that the choice of Mr. John Bracken as our leader was the logical outcome of the policies adopted at the Winnipeg convention, which were perhaps partly inspired by the meeting at Port Hope. What better proof could the Canadian people have of the sincerity of our intentions to put these progressive policies into effect than the selection as our leader of a man whose very name is symbolic of all that we stand for. What he has accomplished over a period of twenty years in the way of progressive legislation and good government in Manitoba, those who know him believe he will succeed in doing in a larger field for the good of all.
I wish to speak for a moment about the seriousness of the farmers' plight. It has already been emphasized by a number of hon. members during the last few days. In my opinion the farmers are the backbone of the country and they have certainly had a raw deal. One-third of the total cost of living is for the food which the farmer produces. Although there is a demand, on account of the war, for all he can produce, he is prevented from making a fair profit which would enable him to pay some of his accumulated debts-perhaps the mortgage on his farm-to improve his equipment and repair his buildings. Farmers work longer hours and receive less return for their labours than anyone else. The increased difficulty they are finding in securing labour, even at a cost two or three times as much as
The Address-Mr. Bruce

it was at the beginning of the war, makes it hai'd for them to carry on even without a profit, and has forced a great many farmers in Ontario, and I am sure elsewhere, to abandon their farms. Old-established herds of dairy cattle have been dispersed, and the farmers have had to sell their implements, often at a loss, and abandon their farms because they cannot possibly carry on as a result of lack of labour, and in addition, through lack of ability to make both ends meet. All of this would have been avoided had the government courageously adopted compulsory selective service in 1940. Thirty-one per cent of Canada's population consists of farmers whose average annual income in the fifteen years prior to 1940 was one thousand dollars. To-day the farmer's least experienced helper can leave him and get work in a munitions factory for double the wages which the farmer can afford to pay.
In this country, the primary industry of which has been farming, we have had bacon, beef and butter shortages. These shortages have been explained by the necessity of sending large quantities of these products to England. This, in my opinion, is a very unfair excuse. Surely, in a great agricultural country like Canada, if we had had proper planning there would have been ample supplies, not only for Great Britain but for ourselves, without rationing.
I wish to say a word about nutrition. In a letter from the Prime Minister, published as an advertisement in the press under the heading "Canada's nutrition programme", we are told that every effort has been made by the government to ensure that, despite war conditions, there shall be an adequate supply of essential foods for all our people. But the speech from the throne speaks only of exploring the farm situation. These two statements do not tally. Exploring will not give the working man a lunch-pail with good beef sandwiches made with buttered bread, or a good rasher of bacon for his breakfast. These things he is at present unable to get in spite of the nutrition programme heralded by the Prime Minister. What use is it to tell people what nutritious food they should eat when they are unable to procure this food? It is on a par with another government advertisement from the salvage department asking housewives to save fats, and thereby assist in providing forty million pounds of needed fat, when they cannot buy bacon or pork and only a limited amount of beef from which they could secure such fat. It does not quite make sense.
Since bread is still the staff of life, it is highly desirable in these days, particularly

when there is a food shortage, that we should see that all our citizens get bread, but bread of the highest nutritional value, especially in so far as essential vitamins are concerned. May I suggest to the government that they establish still another control, and make it illegal for bakeries to offer for sale more than the two types of bread which meet this requirement, namely, first, vitamin B, white bread, Canada approved, and second, whole wheat bread. As to the respective food values of different kinds of bread, the public are hopelessly at sea, and since it is in the national interest that our citizenry maintain a high standard of health and efficiency by eating the most nutritious foods, this can be assured them only by making it impossible for them to purchase any other kind. The most nutritious breakfast cereal is the old-fashioned coarse oatmeal upon which our Scottish ancestors were brought up, and yet it seems a strange circumstance that one cannot buy coarse oatmeal in any grocery store in Ottawa or Toronto, so I am informed. One can, however, secure this oatmeal in feed stores at six cents a pound, and it is not only a nutritious food but the most palatable of all breakfast cereals.
There are a great many prepared foods made and put on the market. Many emanate from Battle Creek and other places, and the only value in them is that they act as a vehicle to convey real food in the form of cream or milk to the individual who eats them. Nevertheless, on account of the tremendous amount of advertising, they have not only fooled the public into purchasing them as beneficial food but have made huge fortunes for those who invented them.
Growing dissatisfaction about food shortage has resulted in a demand made in this house by several members for a ministry of food. While I agree that something should be done in this regard, I do not agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck), or the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) should fill this post. Shortage of food for civilian consumption in this great agricultural country constitutes a national emergency of the first magnitude. It has been emphasized over and over again that one of our greatest contributions to the war should be supplying foods to Great Britain and our allies as well as to the countries of Europe and Africa which will soon, I hope, be liberated from nazi domination. It is hardly necessary to say that this food scarcity is the result of a shortage of farm labour, and this in turn has been caused by the muddling of man-power

The Address-Mr. Bruce
by a government which I fear thought more of its political future than of the welfare of the country, and refused to face the issue of compulsory selective service. This manpower muddle called forth from Mr. Elliott Little, the former director of selective service, the statement to which the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) referred this afternoon, namely, that in the fourth year of war we find ourselves with no clear direction from the government on man-power policy, and with quite inadequate organization to achieve a total and balanced war-power effort.
The resignation of Mr. Charles Yining from the wartime information board causes one to reflect upon the type of information which would be of the greatest value to us in the United States. Most of us recall that after the last war the question of war debts owing to the United States was used as a reason for isolationism. We know there is a great deal of criticism of Canada in the United States owing to the refusal of our government to send draftees for service wherever the enemy is to be found, whereas in the United States, after Pearl Harbor, this was immediately put into effect. This criticism has been accentuated as the war goes on and will place Caanda in an unfavourable position at the peace table if it continues.
Is it fair to our war industries, to our farmers, or to our forces to continue this vacillating policy of political expediency when our very existence is imperilled? Farmers are asked to produce more food this year than they did last year; yet they have more difficulty with labour this year than they had last, and therefore, I fear, they will be able to produce much less. One cannot turn farm production on and off like an electric current by turning a switch. No amount of manpower can produce sides of bacon in less than a year. Although operating a farm I speak for a city constituency, which will be the first to suffer from a food shortage. The city consumer therefore is vitally interested in the farm labour problem. The city consumer includes workers in our industries, and they as well as the soldiers and airmen need an abundance of food. Does not the cutting of the army ration by twenty-five per cent recently indicate that we are close to a serious shortage of food? This problem must be met and met immediately if the situation is not to deteriorate still further and if we are not to let Great Britain and our allies down. It gets back to the problem of our having two armies, one overseas and the other of ho,me defence draftees, which again is the result of the government's unwillingness to impose compulsory selective service.
I therefore suggest as an emergency measure that all those draftees in the home defence army who will not go active be put into a labour battalion, distributed among the farmers on April 1 next and remain on the farms until the crop is harvested in the fall. At the present time they constitute a waste of manpower; they are not helping to win the war; but in a labour battalion, helping in the production of food, they would be usefully employed in a war industry. If by any chance there are more than enough to supply the farm needs, the surplus could be used in some other war industry, but since our farms are said to have been drained of 250,000 men I doubt whether there would be much of a surplus.
The greatest promise that we can hold out to the starving conquered countries of Europe is that of providing them with food as soon as they are liberated. What faith will they have in our promises when they learn that we have had to ration ourselves, that even here there is not enough food to go round?
I have just to-day received an answer to a question I put on the order paper at the beginning of the session, regarding a report which is alleged to have been presented to the government or to some of its key men here in October, 1940, by Mr. Charles Burton, president and general manager of the Robert Simpson Company Limited, Toronto, on the vital question of food supply. I have just received sessional paper No. 146 purporting to reply to my question. It consists of twenty-one pages, and I submit that this is a great waste of material in war time. Each sheet duplicates the same question and has taken up the time of some official, and they are all answered in the same way, "no", or "nil". If we had adopted in this house or adopted now the suggestion made a few days ago by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) that there should be a change in the procedure of the house so that questions could be submitted one evening and the next day ministers would give their answers in the house, this would be much more satisfactory. If they had given this answer to me to-day, I would then have asked them if this plan was not submitted to some of the key men in their departments, and I venture to say that the answer would not have been no, because I think it is a well-known fact that there was such a plan submitted. As a matter of fact I have a copy of that plan and should like to have it put on the record if Mr. Speaker will allow me to do so.
Mr. Burton made this report after wide travelling in western Canada during which he made a study of the whole economic situation
The Address-Mr. Bruce

and all possibilities through the channels open to a company which sells to and buys from all types of Canadians throughout the dominion. Although there are many able men in Canada, it is doubtful if any of them get the clear view of what is happening or will happen economically in every part of the country that is obtained by a man whose managerial ability has placed him at the head of a great institution such, as Simpson's or Eaton's. Such a man has to know, and his advice in keeping Canada solvent cannot be lightly disregarded. President Roosevelt recognized this fact when he conscripted Donald Nelson, one of America's greatest buyers and sellers, to help his government.
Will you call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker? I am now going on to another subject.

I will say just a few words now and then discontinue.
The munitions industry has been organized single-mindedly for output, and I should like to say, successfully organized. Why cannot we do the same thing for food? When we hear proposals for a ministry of food it should be clear that the matter is urgent. Mr. Burton's plan of wheat disposal was intended to hasten the solution of other problems as well. He suggested using the enormous surplus of wheat to produce animal food. I ask the government why this plan was ignored, even though it was only presented to some of the key men belonging to some of the ministries? It would seem that this country is being run like a big business without a general manager.
